clue.text: Detective and another inside corner outlaw

indicators.note: inside means within the walls of something, so one part is set into the middle of a longer word

blocks.note: dick is old slang for a private eye
to corner is to turn, as a car does
another detective: a PI, private investigator

explanation.surface: Two sleuths team up to trap a criminal in a tight spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' only makes sense as another of the thing just named, so it is a second sleuth, the private investigator; 'corner' is a verb, as when a car takes a bend.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick Turpin was a notorious eighteenth-century English highwayman, a famous robber of coaches on the roads.

clue.text: Worn peg securing new articles

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so the outer word holds the others inside it

blocks.note: a dowel is a wooden peg
standard abbreviation for new
the indefinite article A and the definite article THE

explanation.surface: An old peg is holding together some fresh pieces of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' means grammatical articles, both the indefinite and the definite one, not pieces of writing; 'Worn' at the front is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shabby and shoddy in appearance, like shoes whose heels have worn away; an idiom for looking poor and neglected.

clue.text: Around left one, a leg support

blocks.note: ca. is circa, Latin for around
standard abbreviation for left
the Roman numeral for one
a, as in 'five pounds a head', means per

explanation.surface: Someone describes where to fit a brace around a single limb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a placement instruction but is the abbreviation CA, and 'a' must be read as PER, as in a price per item.
explanation.definitionFit: A caliper is a metal brace strapped to a weak or injured limb to hold it straight and bear weight.

clue.text: Romeo appears in art from poet – with explosively hot 26 Across of 9 Across about 20 Down's 10 Across?

annotation.answer: THE PORTRAIT OF MR W H

definitions.text: 26 Across of 9 Across about 20 Down's 10 Across

indicators.note: an explosion scatters everything, so the letters are blown apart and land in a new order

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A lover turns up in a poet's work, accompanied by something fiery.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is built from other answers: a WORK (26) of WILDE (9) about THE BARD's (20) OBSESSION (10); Wilde's story speculates on the young man of Shakespeare's sonnets.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde's 1889 story explores the theory that Shakespeare's sonnets were addressed to a boy actor called Willie Hughes.

clue.text: What may support case for changing amps in Zeppelin music?

indicators.note: letters that are changing are being rearranged into a new order
to be in something is to sit within it, so these pieces go inside the outer word

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
A is the symbol for amperes
Led Zeppelin were a rock band

explanation.surface: A roadie wonders what holds the flight case when swapping amplifiers at a Led Zeppelin gig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case for' reads as a phrase about luggage, but 'for' is the fodder to be rearranged; Led Zeppelin's genre then wraps round the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A rack fixed on top of a car carries luggage such as suitcases, so it is one thing that may hold a case up.

clue.text: Members elected first make persistent demands

blocks.note: the ins are the members of the party voted into office
1st, with the numeral read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Newly elected representatives immediately start lobbying hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ins' is a dictionary term for those in power, as in the ins and outs; 1ST is written with I for the digit.
explanation.definitionFit: To insist is to keep demanding something firmly and refuse to back down; a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: See 3
Abandoned male expelled from brood

indicators.note: whatever is expelled is thrown out, so one letter is removed from the longer word

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for male
to brood is to ruminate, mulling things over

explanation.surface: A cock bird is thrown out of the nest and left to fend for itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brood' looks like a noun, a nest of chicks, but it is the verb ruminate; RUINATE is an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruinate is an old adjective meaning ruined or fallen into decay, as a derelict, deserted building is.

clue.text: One making suggestion: deliver the sticks?

blocks.note: someone who hints
to land a blow is to deliver it

explanation.surface: Someone proposes bringing the firewood round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The sticks' looks like the thing being delivered, but it is the definition, slang for remote countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: The sticks is informal for rural back country far from towns, which is what a hinterland is.

clue.text: Tempestuous in speech getting an Oscar

indicators.note: in speech means spoken out, so we go by the sound of the word, not its spelling

blocks.note: tempestuous means stormy or wild

explanation.surface: A stormy speech wins someone a film award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' suggests the Academy Award, but here an Oscar is anyone with that first name, and the famous one is the Irish writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright and wit, is one person who bears that first name.

clue.text: Fixed idea from alumnus prior to meeting

blocks.note: an old boy of a school
a session is a sitting or meeting

explanation.surface: A former pupil had a fixed notion before going into a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: OB, old boy, is the British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: An obsession is a thought that occupies the mind constantly and cannot be shaken off, an idée fixe.

clue.text: Pig Enigmatist groomed for show

indicators.note: grooming tidies and rearranges things, so these letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; an enigmatist is a setter of puzzles

explanation.surface: A pig, or a crossword setter called Enigmatist, is spruced up for exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: Enigmatist is the pseudonym of a well-known Guardian setter, so the surface reads as a jibe; the definition is a British TV programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Spitting Image was a satirical British television series of the 1980s and 1990s using latex caricature puppets.

clue.text: Stall for box enclosing a small container

indicators.note: to enclose is to surround, so the outer word wraps round the rest

blocks.note: pro is Latin for for, as in pros and cons
a crate is a box
taken as written
standard abbreviation for small
a tin is a container

explanation.surface: A market trader keeps a stall to sell boxes that hold little tins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stall' reads as a noun, a market stand, but is the verb meaning to delay.
explanation.definitionFit: To stall is to play for time and put off action, which is exactly what procrastinating means.

clue.text: Device once used to achieve digital compression?

definitions.text: Device once used to achieve digital compression?

blocks.clueFragment: Device once used to achieve digital compression?
blocks.note: surface reading: an obsolete gadget for compressing digital data, like a file or audio
setter's reading: digital means of the fingers, so this is squeezing a digit, as an old torture instrument did

explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital compression' sounds like computing, but digital also means relating to fingers; the device crushed a prisoner's digit.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval instrument of torture clamped a victim's fingers or toes and was tightened to crush them.

clue.text: Horse brought across turbulent Dart – Sea Biscuit?

indicators.note: something brought across spans the rest, its two ends on either side
turbulent water churns things around, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: a hack is a riding horse
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A horse is led over the rough river Dart; is it the famous racehorse Seabiscuit?
explanation.walkthrough: Seabiscuit was a champion US racehorse, which suits 'Horse'; the Dart is a Devon river. Split, 'Sea Biscuit' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardtack is a hard, dry ship's biscuit that kept for long voyages and fed sailors at sea.

clue.text: See 1
Firm British sailors base in Sandwich – fertile territory?

indicators.note: in places one thing within another, so one letter is set within the filling of the next piece

blocks.note: abbreviation for company
the Royal Navy
e is the base of natural logarithms
bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich

explanation.surface: A British naval company sets up base in the Kent port of Sandwich, rich farmland.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandwich is a town in Kent, which makes 'base' look like a naval station; read as a lunch, it is a BLT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Corn Belt is the American Midwest region whose rich soil makes it the main maize-growing area of the country.

clue.text: In US fall back – line showing any number lost? It's common

indicators.note: going back means going the opposite way, so the word is read from end to start
something lost has gone missing, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: Americans say fall for the season Britons call autumn
n stands for any number in algebra
standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Someone notices that in America the clocks fall back, and that this is normal there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall back' suggests putting clocks back in autumn; here fall is the American season name, reversed, then N goes and L follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutual means shared by two or more parties, as in a mutual friend, which is a sense of common.

clue.text: Write cryptically about books with separate categories

indicators.note: done cryptically means in a puzzling, coded way, so the letters are scrambled
about means around, so these letters surround the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the Old Testament, a collection of books

explanation.surface: A setter is told to write puzzles about literature, sorting them into different groups.
explanation.walkthrough: OT, the Old Testament, is a standard crossword source for books.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-tier system divides things into two distinct levels or classes, so it has separate categories.

clue.text: Quipping commentator tense visiting lexicographer

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's home, so this letter enters the other word

blocks.note: Samuel Johnson compiled the famous 1755 English dictionary
standard grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A witty broadcaster is nervous about calling on a dictionary-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for the commentator's nerves but is the grammar abbreviation T.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Johnston was a BBC cricket commentator on Test Match Special, beloved for his jokes and on-air puns.

clue.text: Lauded writer in time was told about book

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for time
if you were told something, you heard it
standard abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A famous author learnt, in time, about a book being praised.
explanation.walkthrough: T comes first, then HEARD wraps round B; the result is the nickname for Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare is universally praised and known by the nickname the Bard of Avon, a celebrated poet and playwright.

clue.text: Break cover, say, with repairers in service sent north

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading north means travelling upward, so the letters run bottom to top

blocks.note: e.g., for example
REME, the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, mends the British Army's kit

explanation.surface: Army mechanics posted up north leave their hiding place.
explanation.walkthrough: REME is the British Army corps that maintains equipment, hence repairers in the service.
explanation.definitionFit: To break cover is to come out from a hiding place into view, which is to come out or appear.

clue.text: Playing fairly in Pointless with mark adjusted

indicators.note: something adjusted has been altered and set differently, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written; Pointless is a BBC TV quiz show
taken as written

explanation.surface: A contestant on the BBC quiz Pointless plays fair after their score is corrected.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics flag Pointless as the title of a British TV quiz show; it is used purely for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportsmanlike describes conduct that is honourable and fair to opponents, the way good sports behave in any game.

clue.text: Fly low, rising after sharp bends?

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom upward, which flips the word

blocks.note: the letter's zigzag shape resembles a pair of sharp bends, as on a road sign
to low is to moo like a cow

explanation.surface: A plane flies low, then climbs steeply after tight turns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly low' looks like one phrase about flying; it splits into the definition and the cow's noise.
explanation.definitionFit: To zoom is to move very fast, and in aviation it means to climb steeply, so it is a kind of flying.

clue.text: Control with straps supporting church buttress

blocks.note: reins are straps used to control a horse
to be for something is to support it
Church of England

explanation.surface: Builders shore up a church with straps to hold its walls in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' and 'buttress' both look like building terms; the first is the word FOR, the second the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To buttress something is to prop it up and strengthen it, which is a synonym for making it stronger.

clue.text: Battle here happening, gutless duke flees

indicators.note: without guts means without the middle, so only the outside letters stay
whatever flees runs away, so those letters leave the word

blocks.note: à la mode means fashionable, and happening is slang for trendy
just the outside letters of the word

explanation.surface: A cowardly duke runs away from a fight going on right here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happening' reads as a verb but is the adjective meaning fashionable; removing the D and E from A LA MODE leaves the fort.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alamo, a mission fort in Texas, was the site of a famous 1836 siege and battle; it is a place where fighting happened.

clue.text: Job getting rook into frying-pan

indicators.note: putting something into another thing places it inside, so one letter goes within the other word

blocks.note: R is the chess abbreviation for rook
a wok is a Chinese frying pan

explanation.surface: A cook is tasked with getting a crow into the pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' is the bird in the surface, but here it is the chess piece, abbreviated R.
explanation.definitionFit: Work and job are everyday synonyms for employment or a task to be done.

clue.text: Husband misused methadone in area outside church

indicators.note: something misused is put to the wrong purpose, so the letters are rearranged wrongly

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for husband
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A husband abuses a heroin substitute somewhere outside a church.

explanation.definitionFit: Heathendom is the realm of those who are not Christian, the world lying beyond the faith of the church.
